doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Learning tunes and the Sydney Conservatorium
summary: Bucky Pizzarelli's push for repertoire, her two years at the conservatorium with Mike Nock and Don Burrows, and the five Newcastle friends who became professionals.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: How do you learn all the tunes that you need to know as a bass player? And you must have to tell your students something about that.

Well, it’s funny, sometimes there’s two schools of thought in jazz. Bucky Pizzarelli, when he was at William Paterson, boy, I mean I knew some that studied with him, he really got on kids’ cases. I think Bucky can do it and get away with it, he’s just so wonderful. He’d get on kids’ cases about learning tunes and having repertoire. I’m not sure if that’s always really the focus in schools. You know what I mean? I’m not sure about that. There was a set repertoire that I had to learn when I was back at the conservatorium, and it was like, I don’t know, maybe 25 tunes a year. I was only there for two years.
Did that education prepare you very well for the real world?

It’s a good question isn’t it. So much of jazz I think is really taught on the bandstand. I’d say yes and no in a way. I had good teachers at the conservatorium. I had great teachers. And you know we’d be playing all the time. You are playing tunes, I was playing tunes back then that I still play on gigs today. I met some wonderful people, Mike Nock, a great piano player who is in New York, was one of my ensemble teachers. Don Burrows, string and jazz legend.

Don Burrows. He’s a string, he’s a legend there, he’s just a great musician, a great guy. He started this jazz course at the Sydney Conservatorium. And I was the first girl student of my bass teacher. It is funny. And he was a great bass player. I don’t know. There’s different ways of — sometimes yeah, sometimes I felt the classes were a waste of time, but I was there with my friends, my sister, and there were five of us from Newcastle that went to the Sydney Con at the same time. We all went to Sydney. Some of us shared a house and we went to the Sydney Con, and all five of us are now professional musicians in different parts of the world. My sister and I are in New York. Adrian Muse is one of the best trombone players in Germany. Andrew Dickenson is a fine drummer, always busy, in Sydney. And then John Foreman, he was the only one that didn’t go with us to the Sydney Con because he was too young, but we had this little group. We had this band together. And he was like 13 at the time, he couldn’t even reach the pedals on the piano. He became the Paul Shaffer of Australia. I mean it was like he had a big MD [Music Director] gig on music shows, he wrote the theme for the Australian Olympics, he’s like the MD for Australian Idol, you know what I mean? He’s like a household name in Australia. I thought that was really wonderful that the five of us from just playing at a jazz camp together and playing music together as like teenagers, actually went to the Con and there was a career. I don’t know what the question was.
